analysis.one_liner: Replaces the mortgage interest deduction with a tax credit and funds affordable rental housing with the savings.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 2017 and referred to two House committees, where it died without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would replace the mortgage interest deduction with a 15% tax credit on up to $500,000 of mortgage debt, and gradually phase the deduction out entirely by 2022. It would spend most of the money the change raises on affordable rental housing: 60% to the national Housing Trust Fund, 30% to rental assistance, and 10% to repair public housing. It would also enlarge the low-income housing tax credit, the program that builds most new affordable rental housing.
analysis.who_benefits: Extremely low-income renters, since the bill's own findings note that only one in four families who qualify for rental assistance receives it and there is a shortage of more than 7 million homes affordable to the bottom 20% of earners. Public housing residents benefit from repair money. Moderate-income homeowners benefit because a tax credit can be claimed even without itemizing, unlike the deduction, which fewer than half of mortgage holders claim today. Co-op owners gain a new deduction for interest and taxes on cooperative land.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the mortgage interest deduction with a 15% credit on up to $500,000 of mortgage debt per residence, so homeowners who do not itemize deductions can get the benefit.

Phases the mortgage interest deduction down from 100% in 2017 to zero after 2021, and lowers the mortgage cap from $1 million to $600,000 over the same period, converting a subsidy skewed to expensive homes into housing money.
Redirects the savings to housing for the poorest families: 60% to the Housing Trust Fund, 30% to rental assistance, and 10% to the Public Housing Capital Fund.
Raises the low-income housing tax credit ceiling from $1.75 to $2.70 per capita and allows a 150% boost for buildings serving extremely low-income households, with inflation adjustments after 2017.

analysis.who_pays: High-income homeowners with large mortgages and owners of second homes, who currently capture most of the deduction's value; the bill's findings state that more than 75% of the deduction's value goes to the top 20% of earners. Treasury general revenues, which are redirected into housing programs.

drawbacks.text: The new credit is nonrefundable, so homeowners with little or no income tax liability get little or nothing from it; the direct homeownership benefit still skews toward taxpayers with taxable income.
Renters get no direct benefit; help for them depends entirely on the redirected savings and on Treasury accurately computing the revenue each year.

Phasing out the deduction on expensive homes could modestly lower prices in high-cost housing markets, a short-term cost to existing owners there, though it could also ease the price pressure that pricing out buyers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design follows what every major tax reform commission has recommended: convert the deduction to a credit and redirect the savings. The main weakness is that the credit is nonrefundable, so the lowest-income homeowners gain little directly, and renters depend on the revenue stream actually being credited. On balance the trade is large: a subsidy worth over three-quarters to the top 20% of earners is converted into aid for the one in four qualifying families who currently receive no rental assistance.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means and Financial Services committees from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, and neither committee ever took it up.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced the bill on February 7, 2017.
It was referred that day to the House Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, the House Financial Services Committee; the action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.
Nine House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
The bill died at the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019, having received no floor action in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income homeowners with large mortgages kept the tax break the bill would have phased out, and no money moved to low-income renters or public housing repairs. The tax-preference status quo, which sends most of the mortgage interest subsidy to the top 20% of earners, survived untouched.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all nine cosponsors were Democrats, and a Republican-controlled House took no action on it; no Republican cosponsored.

industries.industry: Affordable housing developers and LIHTC syndicators
industries.note: The bill raises the low-income housing tax credit ceiling and adds a 150% basis boost for extremely low-income units, making private developers the permanent channel for building subsidized rental housing. Their revenue would grow alongside the public goal of more affordable homes.

Ten percent of the redirected savings would go to the Public Housing Capital Fund to address the more than $26 billion in deferred maintenance cited in the bill's findings, slowing the loss of about 10,000 units a year.

industries.industry: Real estate and mortgage lending serving the high-end market
industries.note: Phasing down the mortgage cap from $1 million to $600,000 and eventually eliminating the deduction reduces the federal subsidy behind jumbo mortgages and second homes on expensive properties.
These households capture more than 75% of the mortgage interest deduction's value under current law; the bill converts that into a capped credit and redirects the difference to low-income renters.
